h1:
Suphan Buri Salee Cake
The Soft, Old-School Souvenir
intro: Ask most people about souvenirs from Suphan Buri and salee cake comes to mind first. Soft and fluffy, with a sweet jasmine-rice scent and bright pastel colours, it is the province's signature sweet, made here since World War II. This article rounds up the long-running salee shops and local sweets that are still actually selling — both in town and at the century-old Sam Chuk Market — with rough prices so you can plan your souvenir run more easily.

blocks.html: Suphan Buri salee cake grew out of the classic steamed cup cake, but with a finer, softer crumb that melts in your mouth. The scent most people know it by is nom maeo (a jasmine-rice fragrance), with pandan, coffee and jasmine versions too. What keeps people hooked is that softness and aroma — but the trade-off is a short shelf life. The original recipe uses no preservatives, so it usually keeps only a few days. If you're buying it as a gift, plan to get it into the recipient's hands quickly.

blocks.text: Salee & souvenir shops the locals recommend

blocks.html: We picked shops that are still genuinely open and that locals mention often, ordered by how original they are and how easy they are to drop by. Prices are rough ranges and shift with size and flavour.

items.name: Mae Buay Salee (Bang Pla Ma)
items.blurb: The original Suphan Buri salee, open since 1942 during World War II. The white nom maeo (jasmine-rice) flavour is the signature — fine, soft crumb, fragrant, and just sweet enough. No preservatives, so it keeps only a few days. It's sold mainly at the shopfront in Bang Pla Ma district, with no Bangkok branch, so if you want the original you have to come to the shop.

items.name: Ekachai Salee Suphan
items.blurb: The largest souvenir centre in the province. It started as a small sweet shop in 1968 and grew into the town's go-to souvenir brand. It sits on the way out of town on the main road, with easy parking. The salee comes in several styles — fresh-milk salee with a Hokkaido-milk scent, filled salee, and crisp-baked salee thip with coconut. Good for one last stock-up before you head home.
items.meta: Edge of town · everything in one stop

items.name: Mae Kim Liang Salee (Sam Chuk Market)
items.blurb: A long-established salee shop inside the century-old Sam Chuk Market — one of the first you'll hit walking in from the market sign. The crumb is soft and gentle, fragrant, with several sizes and flavours to choose from. Good for eating as you wander the market and carrying home as a gift.
items.meta: Sam Chuk Market · near the entrance

items.name: Je Noi Roi Mor Thai Sweets (Sam Chuk Market)
items.blurb: An old Thai-sweets shop in front of the riverside coffee shop. Je Noi has been making sweets since she was young, cooking fresh each day — around a hundred pots a day, which is where the name (roi mor, 'hundred pots') comes from. There's a wide range of Thai sweets, now portioned into bags at friendly prices, so it's easy to grab several to sample together.
items.meta: Sam Chuk Market · made fresh daily

items.name: Chuang Heng Salted-Egg Mooncake (Sam Chuk Market)
items.blurb: A mooncake (khanom pia) shop over 60 years old in Sam Chuk Market. Packed fillings, several to choose from, with the salted-egg version as the star. The pastry is thin and soft, and it keeps longer than salee, so it's a better bet to carry home over a long distance.

items.name: Khun Aor's Old-Style Khai Pla Sweets (Sam Chuk Market)
items.blurb: A hard-to-find traditional sweet in Sam Chuk Market. It comes in two flavours — yellow for toddy-palm and grey for taro — with a chewy texture and a light sweetness. It's a local sweet that younger generations may rarely see anymore, perfect to sample as you walk the market.

items.name: Old-style snacks in Sam Chuk Market (thong muan, kalamae, mi krop)
items.blurb: Beyond the regular shops, Sam Chuk Market has old-style snack stalls dotted throughout — thong muan (crispy rolled wafers), kalamae (sticky toffee), mi krop (crispy noodles), fresh-butter egg cake, miang kham, and thong yip / thong yot. Most cost a few tens of baht, so you can graze your way around and try several things without sticking to one shop.

blocks.title: Buying tips
blocks.html: The original preservative-free salee keeps only a few days. If you're buying it as a gift to carry far, tell the seller how many days you need it to last — they'll point you to a flavour or recipe that holds up longer. Mooncakes and dry-baked snacks keep longer than fresh salee.

blocks.text: Buy in town, or head to Sam Chuk Market?

blocks.html: If you're short on time and just want some salee to take home, a souvenir shop in town or on the way out — like Ekachai — gets it all done in one stop, with parking and plenty to choose from. But if you want the atmosphere and harder-to-find local sweets, the century-old Sam Chuk Market is the better deal, because you get to wander the old market and sample traditional sweets from several shops in one place.

items.name: Buy in town / on the way out
items.blurb: Good if you're in a hurry — souvenirs all in one shop, with parking, so you can stop before getting on the road home.

items.name: Century-old Sam Chuk Market
items.blurb: An old market that won a UNESCO conservation award, with several traditional-sweet shops — an easy half-day of wandering.

blocks.text: Other local sweets not to miss

items: Salted-egg mooncake — soft pastry with a packed filling, keeps longer than salee, good as a gift to carry far.
Roi mor Thai sweets — Thai sweets made fresh daily at Sam Chuk Market; grab several to sample together at friendly prices.
Thong muan, kalamae & mi krop — dry snacks that keep a long time, easy to find at stalls around the old market.
Old-style khai pla sweets — a rare sweet in toddy-palm and taro flavours; sample one as you walk the market.

faq.q: Which Suphan Buri salee shop is the oldest?
faq.a: Mae Buay in Bang Pla Ma district is considered the original Suphan Buri salee, open since 1942 during World War II. The white nom maeo (jasmine-rice) flavour is the star. It's sold mainly at the shopfront and has no Bangkok branch.

faq.q: How long does Suphan Buri salee keep?
faq.a: The original preservative-free salee usually keeps only a few days. If you're buying it as a gift to carry far, plan to get it to the recipient quickly, or choose dry-baked versions and mooncakes that keep longer.

faq.q: Where is the most convenient place to buy salee?
faq.a: If you want speed, Ekachai Salee Suphan on the way out of town has plenty of souvenirs and parking. But if you want local sweets from several shops plus a stroll, the century-old Sam Chuk Market is the better-value spot.

faq.q: What flavours of salee are there?
faq.a: The most common are nom maeo (jasmine-rice scent), pandan, coffee and jasmine. Some shops also offer fresh-milk salee with a Hokkaido-milk scent, filled salee, and crisp-baked salee with coconut.

faq.q: What local sweets are worth buying at Sam Chuk Market?
faq.a: Besides Mae Kim Liang's salee, there's Chuang Heng salted-egg mooncake, Je Noi's roi mor Thai sweets, and Khun Aor's old-style khai pla sweets, plus thong muan, kalamae and mi krop from stalls around the market.
